1.q: At her appraisal, Joy, a healthcare assistant, is praised by families for her skill in calming people living with dementia who are distressed. Her line manager, Paul, wants to use a strengths-based approach to developing the team. What should Paul do?
o: Concentrate the appraisal on the areas where Joy needs to improve
Move Joy to the dementia unit so that her skills are used there
Ask Joy to spend less time with families so she can do other tasks
Agree a plan for Joy to share her approach and support colleagues
1.w: Strengths-based team development recognises what people do well and builds on it, for example by enabling a team member to share skills and act as a resource, which improves care and motivation (AnnexA.4.2.1; P5.2 strength-based approaches in teams).

n.0: Development needs matter, but a strengths-based approach starts from what the person does well.
n.1: Moving her removes the skill from the team rather than building on it within the team.
n.2: Reducing the activity she excels at undermines a strength that benefits patients and families.

1.q: Jamal, 26, has a moderate learning disability and lives in supported living. Staff report that he has started hitting his head with his hand several times a day. The service manager asks the learning disability nurse what a positive behaviour support (PBS) approach will aim to achieve first. Which answer is best?
o: Refer Jamal to his GP for medication to reduce his agitation and the head hitting
Reduce the behaviour quickly by agreeing consequences that staff apply every time it happens
Keep Jamal safe by planning a restrictive intervention that staff use when he hits his head
Improve Jamal's quality of life by understanding and meeting the needs behind the behaviour
1.w: PBS is a values-led, person-centred framework. It combines a functional understanding of the behaviour with multi-component support whose primary aim is a better quality of life; reduction in behaviour that challenges follows from meeting the person's needs (PBS definition, Gore et al. 2013; NICE NG11 focus on improving support rather than changing the person).

n.0: NICE NG11 places psychological and environmental interventions first; medication is not the first aim of a PBS approach.
n.1: Imposing consequences is a punishment-based approach; PBS changes the environment and support to meet the need the behaviour serves.
n.2: Reactive and restrictive strategies are a last resort within a PBS plan (NICE NG11 1.9.1), not the outcome it sets out to achieve.

1.q: Margaret, 81, has metastatic lung cancer and is being cared for on a medical ward. The team agree she may be in the last days of life and start an individualised care plan. A newly qualified nurse asks how often Margaret should be formally reviewed for changes. Which minimum interval does NICE NG31 recommend for monitoring and updating her care plan?
o: At least every 24 hours
At least every 12 hours
At each weekly multidisciplinary meeting
At least every 72 hours
1.w: NICE NG31 (2015) rec 1.1.6: monitor for further changes in the person at least every 24 hours and update the care plan. Improvement can occur (rec 1.1.3), so regular review guards against wrongly assuming the person is dying.

n.1: Twelve hours is the NG31 minimum for monitoring a person on clinically assisted hydration (rec 1.4.9), not the general review of a dying person.
n.2: A weekly review would miss rapid changes in the last days of life; NG31 asks for monitoring at least every 24 hours.
n.3: Seventy-two hours is too long; NG31 rec 1.1.6 sets a minimum of every 24 hours because the person's condition can change quickly.

1.q: Peter, 68, is two days after bowel surgery. A healthcare support worker reports that he is 'not himself'. You find him drowsy, with snoring respirations and his tongue falling back. Using the ABCDE approach, what is your first action?
o: Open his airway with a head tilt and chin lift and call for help
Check his capillary blood glucose to exclude hypoglycaemia
Review his fluid balance chart and wound drain output
Record a full set of observations and calculate his NEWS2 score
1.w: The ABCDE approach (RCUK) deals with problems in order and treats each one as it is found. Snoring with a falling tongue is partial airway obstruction, which kills fastest, so open the airway with simple manoeuvres and call for help before moving on. Code 15 and P4.10 require a prompt response to deterioration.

n.1: Glucose is checked under D (disability); airway obstruction comes first in the sequence.
n.2: Fluid balance belongs to C (circulation) and does not address the immediate airway threat.
n.3: A full set of observations is useful but delays treating an obstructed airway, which must be dealt with first.

1.t: Physical Health, Transitions and End of Life
1.q: Kieran, 32, has a severe learning disability and epilepsy and lives in supported living. His seizures are hard to describe and staff record them as 'had a funny turn'. What should the learning disability nurse put in place first to improve his epilepsy care?
o: A seizure diary recording each event, its length and recovery
A request for the GP to increase his anti-seizure medicine dose
A daily log of how many hours Kieran sleeps each night
A plan to call 999 for every event that staff witness
1.w: Accurate seizure records (description, time, duration, triggers, recovery, any video with consent) let the specialist judge seizure type and control and adjust treatment. NICE NG217 supports individualised care plans built on accurate information from the person and carers.

n.1: Changing doses without accurate information risks side effects without improving control.
n.2: Sleep can be a trigger worth noting, but it does not describe the seizures themselves.
n.3: An ambulance for every event is not appropriate; his emergency plan should define when to call 999.

1.q: Daniel is a registered nurse on a gynaecology ward. He holds a religious objection to abortion and is allocated to help prepare a patient for a surgical termination of pregnancy this afternoon. Under the Code, what is the most appropriate action?
o: Tell the nurse in charge at the end of the shift that he objects to this work
Tell colleagues, manager and patient, and arrange a qualified colleague to cover
Take part in today's procedure and register his objection with the NMC afterwards
Explain his religious reasons to the patient so that she understands his decision
1.w: Code 4.4: tell colleagues, your manager and the person receiving care about a conscientious objection and arrange for a suitably qualified colleague to take over responsibility for that person's care. Section 4(1) Abortion Act 1967 gives the statutory right to refuse to participate.

n.0: Telling one person after the event leaves the patient's care unplanned; Code 4.4 requires colleagues, manager and patient to be told and cover arranged.
n.2: The NMC does not hold a register of objections; Code 4.4 requires him to declare the objection and hand over care in advance.
n.3: Code 20.7 says not to express personal beliefs to people in an inappropriate way; he must tell her he objects, not argue his beliefs.

1.q: Samuel, a staff nurse on a medical ward, is caring for the family of Daniel, 34, an autistic man without a learning disability who has died after a short illness. Samuel is unsure whether a LeDeR notification is appropriate. What is the correct position?
o: Yes, LeDeR reviews the deaths of autistic people as well as people with a learning disability
No, his death is reviewed by the trust's structured judgement review in place of LeDeR
Yes, but the notification is made by the coroner once the inquest has concluded
No, LeDeR reviews an autistic person's death when a learning disability is also diagnosed
1.w: Since 2021 the programme has been 'Learning from lives and deaths: people with a learning disability and autistic people', so the deaths of autistic adults are reviewed whether or not they also have a learning disability. Anyone, including ward staff and family, can notify a death (leder.nhs.uk).

n.1: A trust mortality review can take place as well, but it does not replace the national LeDeR review.
n.2: Notification does not wait for, or come from, the coroner; anyone can notify LeDeR, including hospital staff and family.
n.3: Autistic people are included in their own right; a co-existing learning disability is not required.

1.q: Rosa, 27, has a moderate learning disability and is being told about her new antibiotic. Which way of speaking is most likely to help her understand?
o: Medical terms explained afterwards in a written leaflet she can keep
A full explanation in one go so that she hears every detail together
A raised voice and slower speech to make sure every word is heard
Short sentences with one idea each, key words stressed and time to respond
1.w: People with a learning disability often need more time to process information. Short sentences, one idea at a time, key words, pauses and checking understanding support communication (Annexe A 1.6; NMC Code 7.1 and 7.4).

n.0: Jargon is a barrier; a leaflet afterwards does not fix an inaccessible explanation.
n.1: Too much information at once overloads processing and reduces understanding.
n.2: Raising the voice does not help understanding unless she has hearing loss and can seem aggressive.

1.q: Sunita, 52, feels well and has no symptoms. After receiving an NHS invitation letter, she attends her GP surgery for cervical screening, and the practice nurse takes a sample. Which level of prevention does this activity represent?
o: Secondary prevention
Health protection
Primary prevention
Tertiary prevention
1.w: Faculty of Public Health, HealthKnowledge: Epidemiological basis for preventive strategies: secondary prevention is the application of available measures to detect early departures from health and to introduce appropriate treatment; screening, such as cervical screening, is a major component.

n.1: Health protection covers measures such as infection control and immunisation, not detecting early disease in individuals.
n.2: Primary prevention controls exposure to risk factors before disease starts, for example immunisation or stopping smoking.
n.3: Tertiary prevention reduces long-term impairment and disability from established disease, such as rehabilitation.

1.q: Priya, a newly registered nurse, arrives for a shift on a surgical ward wearing a long-sleeved cardigan, a wristwatch, a plain metal wedding band and short, unvarnished nails. Before giving direct care, which change does she need to make to meet standard infection control precautions?
o: Remove the cardigan, the watch and the wedding band before patient contact
Keep the cardigan on and swap the wristwatch for a fob watch
Remove the cardigan and the watch and keep the plain wedding band on
Roll the cardigan sleeves to the elbow and wear gloves over the band
1.w: NIPCM ch 1.2: before hand hygiene staff must be bare below the elbows and remove hand and wrist jewellery, with the exception of a single plain metal ring, which should be moved during hand hygiene. Short nails without products are already compliant.

n.0: A single plain metal ring is permitted under NIPCM, so the wedding band does not have to come off.
n.1: Long sleeves stop her being bare below the elbows, so keeping the cardigan on is not compliant even with a fob watch.
n.3: Gloves are not a substitute for hand hygiene, and a pushed-up cardigan is not the bare-below-the-elbows standard.

1.q: Nurse Jo has taught Mrs Akhtar, 70, how to use a new inhaler. Which approach best checks that Mrs Akhtar has understood?
o: Give her a leaflet and ask her to read it tonight
Ask her whether she understands how to use the inhaler
Ask her to show how she will use the inhaler at home
Repeat the explanation slowly a second time
1.w: Annexe A 1.6: check understanding and use clarification techniques. Code 7.4: check people's understanding from time to time to keep misunderstanding or mistakes to a minimum.

n.0: A leaflet supports learning but does not check understanding now.
n.1: A yes or no answer does not show whether she can use it correctly.
n.3: Repetition may help, but it does not check what she has understood.

1.q: Gary, 40, has a mild learning disability. The nurse explains a change to his insulin and asks, 'Do you understand?' Gary smiles and says 'yes', as he does to most questions. What is the best way to check his understanding?
o: Ask him again more slowly whether he understands the change
Give him a printed copy of the instructions and ask him to sign it
Ask his support worker whether Gary has understood the change
Ask Gary to show or tell her in his own words what he will do
1.w: People with a learning disability may agree with questions to please or to avoid looking unsure (acquiescence). Asking the person to explain or demonstrate in their own words checks real understanding (teach-back; Annexe A 1.6 check understanding; Code 7.4).

n.0: Repeating a closed yes or no question is likely to get the same answer.
n.1: A signature on a printed sheet does not show understanding and may be inaccessible.
n.2: His support worker cannot confirm what Gary himself understands.

1.t: Physical Health, Transitions and End of Life
1.q: Oscar, 40, has a learning disability and epilepsy with frequent nocturnal tonic-clonic seizures. He sleeps alone in his flat with no overnight support. Which NICE NG217 recommendation is most relevant?
o: Discuss night-time supervision, such as a night monitor
Wake him every two hours to check whether he is breathing
Ask him to sleep on his back so that seizures are easier to see
Move him to a care home so that staff are on duty every night
1.w: NICE NG217 10.2.1: discuss the possibility of introducing or increasing night-time supervision (for example a night monitor) for people who have seizures during sleep and have been assessed to be at higher risk of epilepsy-related death; living alone and sleeping alone without supervision are modifiable SUDEP risk factors (10.1.2). The discussion respects Oscar's choice and privacy.

n.1: Two-hourly waking disturbs sleep, which can itself trigger seizures, and is not the recommended approach.
n.2: Lying on the back increases the risk of airway obstruction during and after a seizure.
n.3: A move is a major restriction; monitoring can usually be arranged in his own home.

1.q: A practice nurse is planning activities for a GP surgery's prevention week. Which activity is an example of primary prevention?
o: Giving the MMRV vaccine to a child at her one-year appointment
Offering cervical screening to a 30-year-old woman
Sending a bowel screening kit to a 62-year-old man
Referring a man to cardiac rehabilitation after a heart attack
1.w: Faculty of Public Health, HealthKnowledge: Epidemiological basis for preventive strategies: primary prevention is prevention of disease through control of exposure to risk factors. Immunisation prevents infection before it occurs (UKHSA routine schedule from 1 September 2026: MMRV at one year).

n.1: Screening detects early departures from health in people who already have changes, so it is secondary prevention.
n.2: Bowel screening aims to find cancer or polyps early, which is secondary prevention.
n.3: Rehabilitation reduces impairment from existing disease, so it is tertiary prevention.

1.q: In a GP practice, Jamal, a registered nursing associate, is asked to give influenza vaccines at a Saturday clinic. The registered nurses give the vaccine under a patient group direction (PGD). How can Jamal lawfully administer the vaccine?
o: Under a patient specific direction from a prescriber
Under the practice's homely remedy protocol for vaccines
Under the PGD, after signing it as a named practitioner
Under the PGD, while a registered nurse supervises him
1.w: MHRA guidance lists the registered professions that may supply or administer under a PGD (including nurses, midwives, paramedics and pharmacists); nursing associates are not on the list. A nursing associate can administer against a prescription or a patient specific direction from a prescriber.

n.1: Homely remedy protocols apply to non-prescription medicines; influenza vaccine is a POM.
n.2: Signing a PGD does not authorise a profession that the legislation does not include.
n.3: Supervision does not extend PGD use to a profession that is not authorised to use PGDs.

1.q: Mr Okafor, 68, is recovering from a hip replacement and has capacity. After the nurse explains why his evening enoxaparin injection is prescribed and the risk of a blood clot, he says clearly that he does not want it tonight. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Respect his decision, document the refusal and inform the prescriber
Carry out a formal mental capacity assessment before accepting the refusal
Record the omission code on the chart and review at tomorrow's dose
Ask his daughter to visit and persuade him to accept the injection
1.w: Code 2.5: respect, support and document a person's right to accept or refuse care and treatment; Code 4.1 balances best interests with that right. Informing the prescriber allows the VTE plan to be reviewed (Code 13.2 timely referral).

n.1: Capacity is presumed (MCA 2005 s1(2)) and nothing suggests he lacks it; refusing advice is not itself evidence of incapacity.
n.2: Recording the code is part of the answer, but the prescriber must be told so the VTE risk can be reviewed now.
n.3: Recruiting family to pressure him undermines his autonomy; Code 2.5 requires the nurse to respect and support his right to refuse.

1.q: Edna, 79, has metastatic breast cancer and has capacity. The team believe she is entering the last days of life. Her son meets the nurse in the corridor and asks that Edna is not told she is dying because 'it will crush her'. What is the nurse's most appropriate next step?
o: Tell Edna her full prognosis straight away so she is fully informed
Find out from Edna how much she would like to know about her condition
Agree with her son and avoid discussing the prognosis with Edna
Ask the consultant to decide whether Edna should be told she is dying
1.w: NICE NG31 (2015) recs 1.2.1 and 1.2.3: establish how much information the dying person would like about their prognosis, then discuss it with them unless they do not wish to be informed, including those important to them if the person wishes. Priorities for Care (2014): sensitive communication and involving the dying person in decisions.

n.0: This ignores her own preference about how much she wants to know; NG31 rec 1.2.1 asks staff to establish this first.
n.2: Edna has capacity and a right to information; NG31 rec 1.2.3 says discuss the prognosis with her unless she does not wish to be informed.
n.3: The decision about how much information she receives rests with Edna, not with a clinician or relative acting for her.

1.t: Law, Rights and Safeguarding in Learning Disability
1.q: Ravi, 29, has a learning disability. During a capacity assessment about a hernia operation he understands and weighs the information and gives a clear decision, but the next day he cannot remember the discussion. Does his short retention prevent him having capacity for the decision?
o: Yes, because he must be able to write down what he has been told
Yes, because retention for at least a week is needed for surgery
No, because retaining it long enough to make the decision is enough
Yes, because he must be able to recall the information the following day
1.w: MCA s3(3): the fact that a person can retain information relevant to a decision for a short period only does not prevent them from being regarded as able to make the decision. Aids such as an easy read summary can help him later.

n.0: Writing is not required; the test concerns understanding, retaining, using or weighing, and communicating.
n.1: There is no minimum retention period such as a week.
n.3: The Act does not require recall the next day.

1.q: Grace, a student nurse, reads in the revised 2023 LeDeR report that the average age at death of people with a learning disability was 63. She asks her practice assessor how this compared for people with a severe or profound learning disability. Which figure is correct?
o: About 68 years, older than the overall average
About 58 years, younger than the overall average
About 63 years, the same as the overall average
About 48 years, fifteen years below the overall average
1.w: The revised 2023 LeDeR report gives an average age at death of 63 for people with a learning disability, and 58 for people with a severe or profound learning disability, who were also more likely to die of something treatable (LeDeR 2023, republished January 2026).

n.0: People with more severe learning disabilities died younger, not older, than the overall average.
n.2: The report found a clear gap by severity; the average was not the same.
n.3: 48 is too low; the reported average for severe or profound learning disability was 58.

1.q: Nurse Leon is admitting Mrs Clarke, 63, after a bowel resection. He wants to encourage her to describe her recovery in her own words. Which question is most appropriate?
o: "Are you feeling better than yesterday?"
"Have you had any pain since your operation?"
"You're managing well with the pain now, aren't you?"
"How have you been feeling since your operation?"
1.w: Annexe A 1.4: make appropriate use of open and closed questioning. Open questions invite the person to describe their experience in their own words; Code 2.1 work in partnership.

n.0: This closed question limits her to a comparison and a short answer.
n.1: This is a closed question that invites a yes or no answer.
n.2: This is a leading question that suggests the answer she should give.

1.q: A ward is moving from paper charts to electronic observations next month. Several experienced nurses tell Raj, the ward manager, that the system will slow them down and they do not want it. Which approach is most likely to support the change?
o: Ask the nurses who object to work on other wards during the changeover
Involve staff early, explain the reasons, act on concerns and pilot it
Delay the change until every member of the team agrees to it
Set a firm start date and tell staff the system is mandatory from that day
1.w: Effective change management involves the people affected: explaining why the change is needed, listening to and addressing concerns, and testing the change on a small scale so staff can shape it (P5.1 principles of leadership and organisational culture; AnnexA.4.2.1 strengths-based approaches to managing change).

n.0: Removing staff who raise concerns loses their expertise and damages trust in the team.
n.2: Waiting for unanimous agreement can block necessary safety improvements indefinitely.
n.3: Imposing change without engagement tends to increase resistance and workarounds.

1.q: Priya, a student nurse on a community learning disability team, is asked which three features together make up the Valuing People (2001) definition of a learning disability used in England. Which answer is correct?
o: An IQ below 70, an associated physical disability and onset before adulthood
Impaired intelligence, impaired social functioning and onset before adulthood
Impaired intelligence, a known genetic cause and onset before the age of five
Impaired social functioning, onset in childhood and a need for residential care
1.w: Valuing People (DH 2001) defines learning disability as a significantly reduced ability to understand new or complex information and learn new skills (impaired intelligence), with a reduced ability to cope independently (impaired social functioning), which started before adulthood and has a lasting effect on development.

n.0: The definition does not require a physical disability, and an IQ score is not one of its three parts.
n.2: Most people with a learning disability have no identified genetic cause, and the definition sets onset before adulthood, not before age five.
n.3: Needing residential care is not part of the definition; most people with a learning disability live in the community.

1.q: Owen, 19, is autistic and has a learning disability. His PBS plan says that when he begins pacing and repeating 'bus, bus', staff should calmly offer him his picture schedule and a walk outside. Which part of the plan does this describe?
o: Reactive strategies
Primary prevention strategies
Post-incident support strategies
Secondary prevention strategies
1.w: Secondary prevention strategies respond to early warning signs (here pacing and repetitive speech) with de-escalation, such as redirection, reassurance or offering a preferred activity, to stop the situation escalating to a crisis (PBS model).

n.0: Reactive strategies are used once the behaviour is happening to keep everyone safe, not at the early warning stage.
n.1: Primary strategies are proactive and in place all the time, before any early warning signs appear.
n.2: Post-incident support follows an episode (recovery, debrief and review), not the early signs before it.

1.q: A first-year student nurse asks Tom, her practice supervisor, what the Health and Safety at Work etc. Act 1974 requires of her personally as an employee on the ward. Which statement by Tom is correct?
o: You must ensure the health, safety and welfare of all staff on the ward so far as reasonably practicable
You must report every injury you sustain at work directly to the Health and Safety Executive yourself
You must write a formal risk assessment before carrying out each care task that involves any risk to you
You must take reasonable care of yourself and others affected by what you do, and cooperate with your employer
1.w: Section 7 of the Health and Safety at Work etc. Act 1974 places two duties on every employee: to take reasonable care for their own health and safety and that of other people who may be affected by their acts or omissions, and to cooperate with the employer so that the employer can meet its own duties (FACTS S-HSE).

n.0: Ensuring the health, safety and welfare of employees so far as reasonably practicable is the employer's general duty (s2), not the individual employee's duty.
n.1: RIDDOR reports are made by the responsible person (usually the employer); the employee reports the injury through the local incident system.
n.2: Formal risk assessment is an employer duty under the management regulations; employees follow the assessments and safe systems of work their employer provides.

1.q: During induction, a healthcare support worker asks Femi, a staff nurse, when the standard infection control precautions (SICPs) used on the ward should be applied. Which reply from Femi is accurate?
o: To patients having invasive procedures or with invasive devices
To patients with a known or suspected infection or colonisation
To all patients at all times, whether or not infection is known
To patients with diarrhoea, vomiting, fever or an unexplained rash
1.w: NIPCM ch 1 states SICPs are to be used by all staff, in all care settings, at all times, for all patients whether infection is known to be present or not. They reduce transmission from recognised and unrecognised sources.

n.0: Invasive procedures need aseptic technique, but SICPs apply to every patient whether or not a device is present.
n.1: Known or suspected infection triggers transmission-based precautions in addition to SICPs; SICPs themselves apply to everyone.
n.3: These symptoms flag a cross-infection risk for placement decisions, but SICPs are not limited to symptomatic patients.

1.q: Chloe, a registered nurse in a sexual health clinic, sees Zara, 22, who requests emergency hormonal contraception. No prescriber is on site. The clinic has an authorised written direction covering this medicine for defined groups of patients. Under which mechanism can Chloe supply it?
o: A verbal order from an on-call doctor
A homely remedy protocol
A patient specific direction
A patient group direction
1.w: A patient group direction (PGD) is a written direction allowing named, authorised registered professionals such as nurses to supply or administer a specified medicine to a defined group of patients without an individual prescription (MHRA; Human Medicines Regulations 2012).

n.0: Verbal orders are for exceptional changes to existing administration details, not first supply to a new patient.
n.1: Homely remedy protocols cover non-POM medicines in settings such as care homes, not this clinic's POM supply.
n.2: A PSD is an instruction from a prescriber for a named patient after individual assessment; no prescriber has assessed Zara.

1.q: On a leadership study day, students are asked to distinguish leadership from management. Which activity is best described as leadership rather than management?
o: Preparing the ward's off-duty rota for the next four weeks
Setting a shared vision for care and motivating the team
Recording and reviewing staff sickness absence each month
Monitoring the ward's monthly spending against its budget
1.w: Management is concerned with planning, organising and controlling resources (rotas, budgets, absence); leadership is concerned with direction, vision and influencing and motivating people. Nurses need both (P5.1 principles of effective leadership and management).

n.0: Rota planning organises resources, a management task.
n.2: Absence monitoring is a management process.
n.3: Budget monitoring is a management control activity.

1.q: A healthcare assistant asks Sofia, a staff nurse, what the Code means by 'the fundamentals of care' that every registrant must deliver effectively (standard 1.2). Which aspect of care does the Code name as one of the fundamentals?
o: Discharge planning with the wider team
Medicines reconciliation on admission
Wound assessment and dressing selection
Bladder and bowel care
1.w: The note to Code 1.2 says the fundamentals of care include, but are not limited to, nutrition, hydration, bladder and bowel care, physical handling and keeping people in clean and hygienic conditions.

n.0: Discharge planning relates to coordinating care, not to the fundamentals listed in the note to standard 1.2.
n.1: Medicines reconciliation is important but it falls under standard 18 on medicines, not the Code's definition of fundamentals of care.
n.2: Wound care is a clinical procedure; the Code's fundamentals are nutrition, hydration, bladder and bowel care, physical handling and hygiene.

1.t: Physical Health, Transitions and End of Life
1.q: Lily, 23, has a mild learning disability and focal seizures that are not well controlled. She has just started a new relationship and is not using contraception. Her neurologist is reviewing her anti-seizure medicine. Which medicine needs the strictest safety measures because of the risks in pregnancy?
o: Clobazam
Levetiracetam
Lamotrigine
Valproate
1.w: Valproate carries a high risk of birth defects and neurodevelopmental disorders. MHRA measures reflected in NICE NG217 (updated 2025) mean valproate must not be started in anyone under 55 unless two specialists independently document that there is no other effective or tolerated treatment, and a pregnancy prevention programme applies to women and girls who could become pregnant.

n.0: Clobazam is not the medicine with the pregnancy prevention programme.
n.1: Levetiracetam is not subject to the valproate pregnancy prevention programme.
n.2: Lamotrigine is among the options considered for women who could become pregnant; it does not carry valproate's restrictions.

1.q: Amara is a newly registered nurse on a surgical ward in England. During induction a colleague explains that one organisation sets the professional standards in the Code and can take action if a registrant's fitness to practise is impaired. Which organisation is the colleague describing?
o: The Nursing and Midwifery Council
The Royal College of Nursing
The Care Quality Commission
The National Institute for Health and Care Excellence
1.w: The NMC is the professional regulator for nurses, midwives and nursing associates: it publishes the Code (2015, updated 2018), keeps the register and deals with fitness to practise concerns about individual registrants.

n.1: The RCN is a professional body and trade union; it supports nurses but has no regulatory powers over registration.
n.2: The CQC regulates registered providers of health and social care in England (for example enforcing regulation 20, the statutory duty of candour), not individual nurses.
n.3: NICE produces evidence-based guidance; it does not register nurses or judge fitness to practise.

1.q: Frank, 70, says he cannot sleep on the ward because of noise and lights. He is not in pain. Which intervention should be tried first?
o: Move his evening medicines to midnight so that he wakes less
Request a hypnotic medicine for him to take every night
Encourage him to nap during the day to make up for lost sleep
Reduce noise and light at night and offer an eye mask and earplugs
1.w: Annexe B 3.6: support rest and sleep with non-pharmacological measures first, such as a quiet, dark environment, eye masks and earplugs, and a routine. Hypnotics carry risks, including falls in older people.

n.0: Moving medicines to midnight adds a night-time disturbance and may be clinically inappropriate.
n.1: Hypnotics are not first line and increase falls and confusion in older people.
n.2: Daytime napping can worsen night-time insomnia.

1.t: Law, Rights and Safeguarding in Learning Disability
1.q: Adam, 30, has a mild learning disability and lives in his own flat with some support. He has been assessed as having capacity about his diet. He chooses to eat takeaway food most nights despite advice about his weight. What should the community nurse do?
o: Ask his support workers to stop him from ordering takeaway food
Ask the GP to make a best interests decision about his diet
Record that he lacks capacity because the choice harms his health
Respect his decision and keep offering accessible health information
1.w: MCA s1(4): a person is not to be treated as unable to make a decision merely because they make an unwise decision. Adam has capacity, so his choice stands; the nurse continues health promotion in an accessible way.

n.0: Restricting a capacitous adult's choices has no legal basis.
n.1: Best interests decisions are made for people who lack capacity, which Adam does not.
n.2: An unwise choice does not establish a lack of capacity.

1.q: Amara is a newly registered learning disability nurse in a supported living service. Harry, 52, whom she supported for two years, has died in hospital, and her manager says his death will be notified to LeDeR. Amara asks what LeDeR is for. Which description is correct?
o: A coroner's process that decides the legal cause of death and any fault
A police investigation into whether neglect contributed to his death
A service improvement programme that reviews deaths to learn and improve care
A Care Quality Commission inspection that rates the service where he lived
1.w: LeDeR (Learning from lives and deaths: people with a learning disability and autistic people) is an NHS England service improvement programme. Reviews look at the person's life and care to identify learning that improves services and reduces avoidable deaths; it does not apportion blame (LeDeR, KCL national reports).

n.0: Determining the legal cause of death is the coroner's role at an inquest; LeDeR is not a court process and does not find fault.
n.1: Suspected criminal neglect is a police and safeguarding matter; LeDeR is a learning programme, not a criminal investigation.
n.3: CQC inspects and rates registered services; a LeDeR review is about learning from the person's life and death, not rating a provider.

1.q: Kerry, a healthcare assistant, injures her back while helping a patient who began to fall. She is unable to do her normal work for ten days. The ward manager is preparing the RIDDOR report as the responsible person. Within what timescale must the report be made?
o: Within 10 days of the incident
Within 15 days of the incident
Within 7 days of the incident
Within 15 days of her return to work
1.w: Under RIDDOR 2013 an injury that incapacitates a worker for more than seven consecutive days (not counting the day of the accident but including weekends and rest days) must be reported within 15 days of the accident (HSE, RIDDOR: when do I report).

n.0: Ten days is the deadline for the written report of a specified injury or death, not for an over-7-day incapacitation.
n.2: Seven days is the length of incapacitation that makes the injury reportable, not the reporting deadline.
n.3: The 15-day period runs from the date of the accident, not from the worker's return to work.

1.q: Mr Bell, 76, tells the nurse he is 'fine' after hip surgery, but he is grimacing, gripping the bed rail and avoiding eye contact. What is the most appropriate response?
o: "Many people say that after surgery. I'll check on you in an hour."
"You say you're fine, but you look uncomfortable. Can you tell me more?"
"Are you sure? Shall I fetch you some painkillers to be safe?"
"That's good to hear. Let me know if anything changes later on."
1.w: Annexe A 1.1: actively listen, recognise and respond to verbal and non-verbal cues. Code 2.6: recognise when people are anxious or in distress and respond compassionately.

n.0: This dismisses the cues and delays assessment of possible pain.
n.2: Offering analgesia without assessment skips exploring what he is experiencing.
n.3: This accepts the verbal message and misses the non-verbal cues of pain.

1.q: You are caring for Harold, 78, who is in a side room with confirmed Clostridioides difficile diarrhoea. You have just helped him to the commode and removed your gloves and apron. What is the most appropriate method of hand hygiene now?
o: Apply alcohol-based handrub, rubbing all surfaces for 20 to 30 seconds
Use a detergent hand wipe, then apply alcohol-based handrub
Rub hands with an antimicrobial surgical scrub solution until dry
Wash with liquid soap and running water, then dry with paper towels
1.w: NHS England NIPCM (ch 1.2) says wash hands with non-antimicrobial liquid soap and water when caring for a patient with a suspected or known gastrointestinal infection, such as a spore-forming organism like C. difficile. Alcohol does not reliably act against spores, so mechanical removal by washing is needed.

n.0: Alcohol-based handrub is the routine method, but it is not effective against C. difficile spores, so NIPCM directs soap and water here.
n.1: Hand wipes followed by handrub are a fallback for when running water is unavailable; Harold's side room has running water.
n.2: Surgical scrub products are for surgical hand antisepsis before sterile procedures, not routine care of a patient with C. difficile.

2.q: Arthur, 82, is in a four-bed bay and needs help to use a commode. The curtains around his bed space do not fully close and a visitor is sitting at the next bed. Which action best protects his privacy and dignity?
o: Help him quickly so that he is exposed for as short a time as possible
Delay the commode until visiting time has finished in an hour
Ask the visitor to look away while you help him onto the commode
Close the gap with a dignity clip and tell him before starting
2.w: Annexe B 3.4 requires privacy and dignity at all times, and Code 1.1 requires dignity in all care. Secure the screens fully (for example with dignity clips) and explain what you are doing before starting personal care.

n.0: Speed reduces exposure but leaves him visible through the gap.
n.1: Delaying elimination is uncomfortable, undignified and risks incontinence.
n.2: Relying on a visitor to look away does not provide privacy.

2.q: Doreen, 79, is fluid overloaded with worsening breathlessness. The registrar, who is scrubbed in theatre for the next 2 hours, phones the ward to add a single dose of intravenous furosemide now. Trust policy permits verbal orders in exceptional circumstances. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Accept it per policy and ask for written confirmation within 7 days
Refuse, and wait for the registrar to write it after theatre
Write the new dose on the drug chart herself and sign it as the prescriber
Accept it per policy and ensure written confirmation, ideally within 24 hours
2.w: RPS/RCN guidance (2019) para 20: in exceptional circumstances, where delay would compromise care and the medicine is not a Schedule 2 CD, verbal orders may be used under organisational policy; the prescriber then amends the chart or provides a prescription as soon as possible, ideally within 24 hours.

n.0: The RPS/RCN standard is ideally within 24 hours, not 7 days.
n.1: A 2-hour delay could compromise Doreen's care when policy allows a verbal order.
n.2: Transcribing cannot be used to add a new medicine; the nurse would be acting as an unauthorised prescriber.

2.t: Law, Rights and Safeguarding in Learning Disability
2.q: Josh, 25, has a moderate learning disability and is refusing a blood test on the medical ward. The doctor says, 'He has a learning disability, so he can't consent; just do it in his best interests.' What is the most appropriate response by the nurse?
o: Ask his mother to give consent for the test as his next of kin
Explain that capacity is assessed for this decision, not assumed from diagnosis
Agree, as a moderate learning disability means he cannot weigh up information
Agree, as a blood test is a minor procedure that needs no consent
2.w: MCA 2005 s1(2): a person must be assumed to have capacity unless it is established that they lack it; s2(3): lack of capacity cannot be established merely by reference to a condition. Capacity is decision-specific and must be assessed for this blood test.

n.0: A next of kin cannot consent for an adult without a relevant LPA or deputyship.
n.2: A diagnosis of learning disability never by itself establishes lack of capacity.
n.3: Every intervention, including a blood test, needs valid consent or another lawful basis.

2.q: Amira, 45, has pneumonia. On assessment her airway is clear. Her respiratory rate is 28 breaths per minute and SpO2 is 89% on air. She has no history of lung disease. According to the ABCDE approach, what should you do next?
o: Give oxygen to achieve a target saturation of 88-92% and summon help
Move straight on to assess her pulse, blood pressure and capillary refill
Give oxygen to achieve a target saturation of 94-98% and summon help
Ask her to take deep breaths and recheck her saturation in an hour
2.w: Problems found under B are treated before moving to C. For acutely ill adults not at risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure the target is 94-98% (BTS; NICE NG253 rec 1.10.1), so start oxygen and get help early.

n.0: 88-92% is the target for people at risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure, which Amira is not.
n.1: ABCDE requires treating the breathing problem found at B before assessing circulation.
n.3: An hour's delay with SpO2 89% and RR 28 leaves hypoxaemia untreated.

2.q: Mrs Holt, 80, has advanced dementia and limited speech. During a wash she grimaces, guards her left hip and pulls away when touched there. She cannot say whether she is in pain. How should the nurse interpret these findings?
o: As refusal of care, so the wash should be abandoned
As non-verbal signs of physical distress that need assessment
As features of her dementia that need no further action from staff
As agitation that should be treated with a sedative
2.w: Annexe B 1.2.2 requires nurses to recognise symptoms and signs of physical distress. In people who cannot report pain, behaviours such as grimacing, guarding and withdrawal may indicate pain, so the hip should be assessed further (for example injury from a fall) using an appropriate observational tool.

n.0: Stopping the wash does not address the possible cause of her distress.
n.2: Attributing new behaviour to dementia risks missing a treatable cause such as a fracture.
n.3: Sedation masks the signs and does not treat the underlying cause; assessment comes first.

2.q: According to the NMC Code (2018), which of the following is listed among the fundamentals of care that nurses must deliver?
o: Medicines reconciliation
Discharge planning
Health education
Bladder and bowel care
2.w: Code 1.2 (NMC 2018): fundamentals of care include nutrition, hydration, bladder and bowel care, physical handling and making sure people are kept in clean and hygienic conditions.

n.0: Medicines reconciliation is not one of the Code's listed fundamentals.
n.1: Discharge planning is important but is not in the Code's list of fundamentals.
n.2: Health education is not in the Code's list of fundamentals of care.

2.q: Ahmed, 72, has end-stage COPD and is on a respiratory ward. He is thought to be in his last days. He tells the nurse he wants to die at home, and his wife says she wants this too and can stay with him. What should the nurse do first?
o: Explain that moving him home in the last days of life is not safe for him
Ask the GP to decide whether a home death would be appropriate
Start arranging the equipment, care and medicines needed at home without delay
Record his wish and review it at next week's multidisciplinary team meeting
2.w: NICE NG31 (2015) recs 1.3.4 and 1.3.5: establish as early as possible the resources needed (equipment, care at night, support) and create an individualised care plan that includes the person's preferred care setting. Priority for Care 5: an individual plan of care agreed and delivered with compassion.

n.0: NG31 supports a preferred care setting where possible; transfer is not ruled out simply because he is dying.
n.1: The plan is made with Ahmed, his wife and the multidisciplinary team; deferring the decision to the GP delays action on his wish.
n.3: Waiting a week risks him dying before his wish can be met; NG31 rec 1.3.4 says establish resources as early as possible.

2.q: Priya, a newly registered nurse on a surgical ward, is reading the Code during her preceptorship. She wants to know which of the four themes contains the standard on keeping clear and accurate records. Which theme is it?
o: Promote professionalism and trust
Prioritise people
Practise effectively
Preserve safety
2.w: The Code (NMC 2015, updated 2018) has four themes: Prioritise people (1-5), Practise effectively (6-12), Preserve safety (13-19) and Promote professionalism and trust (20-25). Standard 10, keep clear and accurate records, sits under Practise effectively.

n.0: Promote professionalism and trust covers standards 20-25 (reputation, registration, investigations, complaints, leadership), not record keeping.
n.1: Prioritise people covers standards 1-5 (dignity, preferences, needs, best interests, confidentiality); records sit under standard 10.
n.3: Preserve safety covers standards 13-19 (competence, candour, emergencies, raising concerns, medicines, harm reduction); records are standard 10.

2.q: Mrs Fisher, 89, is frail and lives in a care home. Staff report she has become drowsy and less able to feed herself since yesterday. Her temperature is 36.4°C and her urine is cloudy. A colleague says infection is unlikely because she has no fever. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Explain that frail older people may have infection without fever
Ask the care home to collect a urine sample at the next GP visit
Agree, and look for a non-infective cause of her new drowsiness
Agree, and plan to recheck her temperature again in 4 hours
2.w: NICE NG253 (2025) rec 1.4.1: do not rely on fever or hypothermia alone to rule sepsis in or out; rec 1.4.2 notes older or very frail people may not develop a raised temperature, and rec 1.4.9 that cognitive change may present as acute change in function. She needs full assessment and NEWS2.

n.1: Deferring a sample delays assessment of an acute change in an older, frail person.
n.2: Excluding infection on the basis of a normal temperature contradicts NG253 rec 1.4.1.
n.3: Waiting 4 hours for a temperature ignores signs of possible sepsis that need assessment now.

2.q: Mr Achebe, 62, is admitted to a medical ward with poorly controlled type 2 diabetes. The nurse is starting his admission assessment and wants it to be person-centred and shared. Which opening approach best achieves this?
o: Ask his wife to describe his usual routine and difficulties
Review his medical notes and set goals for him to work on
Ask what matters most to him and what he hopes to achieve
Complete the trust checklist, then explain the plan to him
2.w: NMC proficiency P3.4 requires a person-centred approach with shared assessment, planning, decision-making and goal setting; Code 3.3 asks nurses to act in partnership with the person. Starting with what matters to Mr Achebe puts him at the centre of the assessment.

n.0: His wife may add useful information, but he can speak for himself and should be asked first.
n.1: Setting goals for him rather than with him is not shared goal setting.
n.3: Completing a checklist first and then informing him is not shared assessment or decision-making.

2.q: Joseph, a staff nurse, is reviewing a NICE guideline with a student nurse. The student asks what legal status NICE guidance has for registered nurses caring for an individual patient. Which statement by Joseph is most accurate?
o: It replaces individual clinical judgement whenever a recommendation applies
It should be taken fully into account alongside the person's needs and preferences
It carries the same legal force as an Act of Parliament once it is published
It applies to medical staff, while nurses follow local trust policy instead
2.w: NICE's standard 'Your responsibility' statement (seen in NG253) says guidance is not mandatory: professionals are expected to take it fully into account alongside the individual needs, preferences and values of the person. Code 6.1 requires advice to be evidence-based.

n.0: NICE states its guidance supports, and does not replace, the professional's judgement about the individual person.
n.2: NICE guidance is not legislation; it does not have the force of an Act of Parliament.
n.3: NICE guidance applies to all health professionals, including nurses, not to medical staff alone.

2.q: Daniel, 34, had a severe traumatic brain injury at 28 and now needs help with planning, money and personal care. A support worker says Daniel 'now has a learning disability'. Which response by the nurse is most accurate?
o: He meets the definition because intelligence and social functioning are now impaired
He does not meet the definition because his impairment began in adulthood
He does not meet the definition because his impairment has a known physical cause
He meets the definition once the impairment has lasted for more than 12 months
2.w: A learning disability must start before adulthood and affect development (Valuing People 2001). An acquired brain injury in adult life can cause similar impairments but is not a learning disability; Daniel's needs are met under other frameworks.

n.0: Impaired intelligence and social functioning are two of the three parts, but onset before adulthood is missing.
n.2: Many learning disabilities have a known physical cause (for example Down syndrome), so a known cause does not exclude the definition.
n.3: Duration is not a criterion; onset before adulthood is.

2.q: On a medical ward in England, Mr Hughes, 70, was given a tenfold insulin overdose and needed transfer to intensive care. The ward manager asks which organisation regulates the trust's compliance with the statutory duty of candour under regulation 20 of the 2014 Regulations. Which organisation is this?
o: The Care Quality Commission
The Nursing and Midwifery Council
The Health and Safety Executive
The Parliamentary and Health Service Ombudsman
2.w: The statutory duty of candour (Health and Social Care Act 2008 (Regulated Activities) Regulations 2014, reg 20) applies to registered providers and is regulated by the CQC in England. The professional duty in Code 14 is overseen by the NMC for individual registrants.

n.1: The NMC oversees the professional duty of candour of individual registrants (Code 14), not the provider's statutory duty under reg 20.
n.2: The HSE enforces workplace health and safety law such as HASAWA 1974 and RIDDOR, not reg 20 of the 2014 Regulations.
n.3: The Ombudsman investigates unresolved complaints about the NHS; it does not regulate providers' compliance with reg 20.

2.q: Grace, 79, is found by her daughter on the ward to be confused and difficult to rouse. You have assessed and managed her airway, breathing and circulation. Under D (disability), which assessment should you complete?
o: Level of consciousness using ACVPU, pupils and capillary blood glucose
Respiratory rate, chest expansion and oxygen saturation
Pulse, blood pressure and urine output over the last hour
Skin inspection for rashes, pressure damage, wound leakage and drains
2.w: D in the ABCDE approach assesses neurological status: level of consciousness (ACVPU, which NEWS2 uses), pupils and a capillary blood glucose to exclude hypoglycaemia as a reversible cause of reduced consciousness.

n.1: Respiratory rate, expansion and saturation belong to B (breathing).
n.2: Pulse, BP and urine output belong to C (circulation).
n.3: Skin, rashes and wounds are examined under E (exposure).

2.q: Graham, 54, has a BMI of 34 and is at a health check. The nurse explains the health risks of his weight and the support available. Graham says he does not want to change his diet at the moment because of stress at work. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Tell him he must start changing his diet now to avoid a heart attack
Record that he is non-compliant and close the health promotion episode
Refer him to a weight management service even though he has declined
Respect his decision, give information and offer to revisit the topic later
2.w: NMC Standards of proficiency (2018) P2.1 and P2.9: promote health by empowering people to make informed choices, using communication skills and strength-based approaches. NICE PH49 (2014) recommends tailoring interventions to the person's motivation and planning review points; Code 4.1 respects the person's right to accept or refuse.

n.0: Pressuring or frightening him is not empowering; NMC P2.1 and P2.9 support informed choices.
n.1: Labelling him non-compliant is judgemental and closes the door on future support.
n.2: Referral needs his agreement; acting against his choice undermines informed decision-making (Code 4).

2.q: A nurse enters the bay of Gladys, 84, to tidy her over-bed table and move her water jug within reach. Gladys is asleep and the nurse does not touch her. The nurse then turns to leave the bed space. Which of the five moments for hand hygiene applies now?
o: After a body fluid exposure risk in the bed space
Before a clean or aseptic procedure on the ward
After touching a patient's immediate surroundings
After touching a patient during a care episode
2.w: The five moments in NIPCM ch 1.2 are before touching a patient, before clean or aseptic procedures, after body fluid exposure risk, after touching a patient, and after touching a patient's immediate surroundings. Handling the over-bed table and jug is contact with the immediate surroundings, which can be contaminated.

n.0: No blood or body fluid exposure risk occurred while tidying the table.
n.1: The nurse is leaving, not about to start a clean or aseptic task.
n.3: The nurse did not touch Gladys, so the moment 'after touching a patient' does not describe this contact.

2.q: Holly, a student nurse in a community learning disability team, hears her assessor say the team uses a 'total communication' approach. Holly asks what this means in practice. Which description is correct?
o: Using one agreed system, such as Makaton, across all services the person attends
Combining speech, signs, symbols, objects and gestures to suit the person
Replacing speech with pictures for every person who has a learning disability
Asking a speech and language therapist to lead every conversation with the person
2.w: Total communication means using every available channel (speech, signs, symbols, photographs, objects, gestures, body language and technology), tailored to the individual, so the person can understand and be understood.

n.0: Using one system for everyone is the opposite of total communication, which combines methods to suit the person.
n.2: Pictures help some people but not all; total communication adds channels rather than removing speech.
n.3: SLTs assess and advise, but everyone supporting the person uses total communication day to day.

2.q: Ffion, 32, has a severe learning disability and is starting at a new day service. Her family bring a communication passport to her first visit. Staff ask what it is for. Which explanation is correct?
o: It records the legal decisions made in Ffion's best interests
It describes how Ffion communicates and how to communicate with her
It sets out the goals agreed in Ffion's person-centred plan
It records Ffion's medical history and current medicines for staff
2.w: A communication passport is a person-centred document describing how the person communicates (what their sounds, signs and behaviours mean) and how others can best communicate with them, so new staff can understand her quickly.

n.0: Best interests decisions are recorded in the care record under the Mental Capacity Act.
n.2: Goals belong in the person-centred plan; the passport is about communication.
n.3: Medical history and medicines are in the clinical record or hospital passport, not the communication passport.

2.q: During a team teaching session, Kofi, a community learning disability nurse, presents the republished (January 2026) LeDeR report on deaths in 2023. A student asks which causes of death were most common among the people reviewed. Which answer should Kofi give?
o: Dementia, chronic kidney disease and stroke
Cancer, pneumonia and lung infections, and heart conditions
Accidents, suicide and drug or alcohol overdoses
Epilepsy, choking incidents and complications of constipation
2.w: The revised 2023 LeDeR report found the most common causes of death were cancer, pneumonia and other lung infections, and heart problems (LeDeR 2023 report, republished 27 January 2026).

n.0: These causes occur but were not the leading groups in the 2023 report.
n.2: External causes such as accidents and suicide were not among the leading causes for people with a learning disability.
n.3: Epilepsy, choking and constipation still contribute to deaths and are key learning themes, but they were not the most common causes.

2.q: Sam, a community nurse, has just given a subcutaneous injection of enoxaparin to Mrs Ada Kowalski, 69, in her home using a prefilled syringe with a safety device. What is the safest way to deal with the used syringe?
o: Separate the needle from the syringe and place each part in the correct waste stream
Place the used syringe in a rigid tray and dispose of it in the sharps bin in the car
Activate the safety device and place the needle and syringe as one unit in the sharps bin at once
Recap the needle with a one-handed scoop technique and dispose of it at the next clinic visit
2.w: The Health and Safety (Sharp Instruments in Healthcare) Regulations 2013 and the National IPC Manual require safer sharps to be used as designed, no recapping, and disposal at the point of use by the user, with the needle and syringe discarded as one unit into a sharps container (FACTS S-HSE, S-NIPCM).

n.0: Needles must not be disassembled from syringes; the unit is discarded intact.
n.1: Carrying an exposed used sharp away from the point of use increases the risk of injury; a portable sharps container should be taken to the point of use.
n.3: Recapping is a recognised cause of needlestick injury and is prohibited by the Sharps Regulations; carrying a recapped needle to another visit adds further risk.

2.q: Nurse Ola is about to give intravenous co-amoxiclav to Mr Grant, 55, who is alert. Which question type is most appropriate immediately before giving the first dose?
o: An open question about how he feels about his treatment
A reflective question about his previous hospital stays
A closed question confirming any penicillin allergy
A leading question assuming that he has no allergies
2.w: Annexe A 1.4: make appropriate use of open and closed questions. Closed questions obtain specific facts, such as allergy status, quickly and clearly; Code 18 safe medicines practice.

n.0: Open questions are useful for exploring feelings but not for confirming a specific safety fact.
n.1: This does not establish the specific allergy information needed now.
n.3: Leading questions can produce a false answer to a safety-critical check.

2.t: Law, Rights and Safeguarding in Learning Disability
2.q: Mel, 38, has a moderate learning disability and needs a tooth extraction under local anaesthetic. Before anyone concludes that she lacks capacity to decide, which step is most important?
o: Ask her a series of yes or no questions to check her understanding
Give her the standard information leaflet used for all patients
Explain the procedure verbally twice and then ask for her decision
Use pictures and her communication passport, with someone who knows her
2.w: MCA s1(3): a person is not to be treated as unable to make a decision unless all practicable steps to help them have been taken without success. For Mel this means accessible information, her usual communication methods, a supporter who knows her, and the right time and place.

n.0: Yes or no questions risk acquiescence and do not show real understanding.
n.1: A standard leaflet is not accessible for many people with a moderate learning disability.
n.2: Repeating spoken information does not adapt it to her communication needs.

2.q: A learning disability nurse is writing a positive behaviour support plan for Elena, 34, who has a severe learning disability and bites her hand when the day centre becomes noisy. Which strategy is an example of primary prevention?
o: Offering Elena her ear defenders once she starts biting her hand
Moving Elena's activities to a quieter room before the centre gets busy
Recording each biting episode on an ABC chart after it has finished
Guiding Elena's hand away from her mouth when she begins to bite
2.w: Primary prevention strategies are proactive: they change the environment, meet the person's needs and teach skills so that the behaviour is less likely to happen at all. Altering the setting before the known trigger (noise) arises is primary prevention (PBS model; NICE NG11 1.6.1 proactive strategies such as reducing noise).

n.0: Offering a support once early signs or the behaviour have begun is a secondary (de-escalation) strategy, not primary prevention.
n.2: ABC recording is part of functional assessment and monitoring, not a prevention strategy in the plan.
n.3: Physically guiding her hand away during the behaviour is a reactive strategy used to keep her safe.

2.q: Michael, 61, had a stroke three months ago. He now attends community physiotherapy and speech and language therapy to regain function and adjust to living with weakness in his right arm. Which level of prevention does this care represent?
o: Tertiary prevention
Primary prevention
Population prevention
Secondary prevention
2.w: Faculty of Public Health, HealthKnowledge: Epidemiological basis for preventive strategies: tertiary prevention is the application of measures to reduce or eliminate long-term impairments and disabilities, minimising suffering from existing ill health and promoting the person's adjustment to their condition.

n.1: Primary prevention aims to stop the disease occurring at all; Michael has already had a stroke.
n.2: This is a population-wide strategy, not care to reduce one person's long-term impairment.
n.3: Secondary prevention detects disease early in people without symptoms, for example through screening.

2.q: Mr Kim, 71, takes bisoprolol for heart failure. He has pneumonia and his respiratory rate is 24, but his heart rate is 74 bpm. A student nurse says his normal pulse shows he is not seriously unwell. Which explanation should the nurse give?
o: His normal pulse means a sepsis screen is not needed today
Heart rate is the most reliable sign of infection in older adults
Bisoprolol tends to raise the pulse, so 74 bpm is a low reading
Beta-blockers can blunt the heart rate rise with infection
2.w: NICE NG253 rec 1.4.4: interpret heart rate in context; older people may not develop an increased heart rate, and the response may be affected by medicines such as beta-blockers. His raised respiratory rate still needs scoring and escalation as appropriate.

n.0: A pulse in the normal range does not exclude sepsis in someone taking a beta-blocker.
n.1: NG253 warns that older people may not show a rise in heart rate, so it is not the most reliable sign.
n.2: Bisoprolol is a beta-blocker that slows the heart rate; it does not raise it.

2.q: Priya, a newly registered nurse in a community learning disability team, is asked who should be involved in developing a positive behaviour support plan for Mark, 41, who has a moderate learning disability. Which approach is best?
o: Develop it with Mark, his family and the staff who support him day to day
Develop it with the team psychologist, then hand it to staff to put into practice
Develop it with the service manager, who will sign it off for the staff team
Develop it with Mark's GP, who knows his physical health history best
2.w: PBS is person-centred and collaborative: the plan is co-produced with the person, family carers and the staff who support them, because they know the person's needs, triggers and communication and must be able to use the plan consistently (NICE NG11 1.1.1 working in partnership, 1.3.1 involving family in developing the plan, 1.5.2 full involvement in assessment; PBS values).

n.1: Specialist input is valuable, but a plan written by one professional and handed down is not co-produced and is less likely to be used consistently.
n.2: Management sign-off may be part of governance, but involving the manager in place of Mark and his supporters misses the people who know him best.
n.3: The GP's input on physical health is useful, but the GP is not the core partner in designing day-to-day behaviour support.

2.q: Tom, 24, has a learning disability and his community team is discussing whether the Mental Health Act 1983 could apply to him. A student asks how the 1983 Act itself defines learning disability. Which wording reflects section 1(4)?
o: Significant impairment of intelligence present at birth and confirmed by a standardised IQ assessment
A lifelong neurodevelopmental difference in social communication, interaction and sensory processing
Any disorder or disability of the mind associated with abnormally aggressive or seriously irresponsible conduct
Arrested or incomplete development of mind with significant impairment of intelligence and social functioning
2.w: Mental Health Act 1983 s1(4): learning disability means 'a state of arrested or incomplete development of the mind which includes significant impairment of intelligence and social functioning'.

n.0: The Act does not require onset at birth or a standardised IQ test; it refers to intelligence and social functioning together.
n.1: This describes autism, which the 1983 Act does not define in this way and which is distinct from learning disability.
n.2: 'Any disorder or disability of the mind' is the s1(2) definition of mental disorder; the aggressive or irresponsible conduct wording is the separate s1(2A) qualifier.

2.t: Physical Health, Transitions and End of Life
2.q: Jade, 26, has a learning disability and generalised tonic-clonic seizures, some at night. Her mother asks what sudden unexpected death in epilepsy (SUDEP) is and whether anything reduces the risk. Which response is best?
o: Uncontrolled tonic-clonic seizures raise SUDEP risk, and this can be reduced
SUDEP is linked to daytime focal seizures and not to night-time ones
SUDEP risk falls once a person has a learning disability diagnosis
SUDEP is rare, so families do not need to be told about it until later
2.w: NICE NG217 10.1.2 and 10.1.4: discuss SUDEP from diagnosis with the person, family and carers; modifiable risk factors include generalised or focal to bilateral tonic-clonic seizures, uncontrolled seizures, non-adherence, alcohol or drug misuse, living alone and sleeping alone without supervision.

n.1: Tonic-clonic seizures, especially unwitnessed nocturnal ones, are the main risk factors.
n.2: A learning disability does not reduce the risk; people with LD and epilepsy are a higher-risk group.
n.3: NG217 recommends discussing SUDEP risk with people and their families and carers.

2.q: Priya, a registered nurse on a care of older people ward, is preparing to hoist Alan Hughes, 78, from bed to chair. While checking the sling she notices that one of the seams is frayed and partly torn. Two healthcare assistants are waiting to help. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Transfer Mr Hughes by lifting him with the two healthcare assistants instead of using the hoist
Reinforce the torn seam with strong tape and complete the transfer with the hoist as planned
Use the sling for this transfer with an extra person present, then report the damage afterwards
Withdraw the sling from use, label it as faulty, report it and fetch a suitable replacement
2.w: Faulty lifting equipment must be taken out of use and reported so that nobody else uses it, and the planned safe system of work (hoist with an intact sling) should continue with a replacement. This applies the employee duty under s7 Health and Safety at Work etc. Act 1974 to take reasonable care for others, LOLER 1998 (equipment for lifting people must be safe) and Code 19 (preserve safety).

n.0: The Manual Handling Operations Regulations 1992 require hazardous manual handling to be avoided where reasonably practicable; a manual lift of a hoist-dependent person replaces one hazard with another.
n.1: Improvised repairs to lifting equipment are unsafe and conceal the defect; damaged slings must be withdrawn and replaced, not patched.
n.2: An extra person does not make a torn sling safe; using it exposes Mr Hughes to a fall and delays reporting a known hazard.

2.q: During a team meeting, Ellie, a nurse three months after registration, says that leadership is something for ward managers and that her job is to look after her own patients. How does the NMC Code describe leadership for registrants?
o: All registrants have opportunities to show leadership whatever their role
Leadership is required where a nurse is formally in charge of a shift
Leadership is expected once a nurse is appointed to a band 6 role or above
Leadership is expected after completing a recognised leadership course
2.w: Code standard 25 (provide leadership to make sure people's wellbeing is protected and to improve their experiences) applies to every registrant; the NMC states that all registrants have opportunities to show leadership regardless of formal position (P5.6 exhibit leadership potential).

n.1: Being in charge adds responsibilities (Code 25.1), but leadership is expected of all registrants at all times.
n.2: The Code links leadership to professional practice, not to pay band or grade.
n.3: Courses can develop leadership skills, but the Code's expectation does not depend on them.

2.q: Elaine, 45, tells the practice nurse she bought a small pack of paracetamol from a supermarket, but the pharmacy said her prescribed codeine needed a prescription. She asks which legal category allows sale from premises such as supermarkets. Which category is correct?
o: Prescription only medicine (POM)
Controlled drug in Schedule 5
Pharmacy medicine (P)
General sale list medicine (GSL)
2.w: MHRA guidance on medicine categories: GSL medicines can be sold from a wider range of premises, such as supermarkets, if the premises can be closed to exclude the public and the medicines are pre-packed. POM and P medicines are sold or supplied from a registered pharmacy, POMs against a prescription.

n.0: POMs need a prescription and are supplied through a pharmacy or other authorised route.
n.1: Schedule 5 is a controlled drug schedule, not a sale category; such products are sold through pharmacies.
n.2: Pharmacy medicines are sold under a pharmacist's supervision at registered pharmacy premises.

2.q: Mia, 19, has dyslexia. Her general intellectual ability is in the average range, she lives independently and studies at college. Her GP asks the practice nurse whether Mia should be added to the learning disability register. What is the best response?
o: Yes, because the register includes anyone with a special educational need
Yes, because her difficulty with reading began in childhood
No, because she has not yet been assessed by a consultant psychiatrist
No, because she does not have impaired intelligence or social functioning
2.w: The register is for people with a learning disability as defined in Valuing People: impaired general intelligence plus impaired social functioning, starting before adulthood. Mia's average intellect and independent living mean she does not meet the definition; dyslexia is a specific difficulty with one area of learning.

n.0: Special educational needs is an education concept that includes many people without a learning disability; it is not the register criterion.
n.1: Childhood onset is one part of the definition, but Mia lacks the other two parts.
n.2: Psychiatric assessment is not the deciding issue; on these facts she does not meet the definition at all.

2.q: Doris, 76, is unconscious after a stroke and needs her bed linen changed. Two staff are available. Which technique is most appropriate?
o: Roll her to each side in turn, changing half the sheet each time
Lift her out to a chair while the bed is stripped and remade
Change the top sheet and add an extra pad underneath her
Leave the soiled sheet until she regains consciousness
2.w: Annexe B 3.2: bed-making for an unconscious or immobile person is done with the person in the bed, rolling them to each side with enough staff and appropriate handling aids, keeping the airway clear and maintaining dignity.

n.1: Transferring an unconscious person to a chair is unsafe and unnecessary.
n.2: Adding pads over soiled linen leaves her lying on moisture and risks pressure damage.
n.3: Leaving soiled linen risks skin damage and infection and is undignified.

2.q: Mr Rahman, 58, is a practising Muslim admitted for a planned operation in England. He asks the nurse whether he can be helped to pray at the set times each day and have a quiet space to do so. Which Article of the Human Rights Act 1998 Schedule 1 most directly protects this request?
o: Article 9, freedom of thought, conscience and religion
Article 14, the prohibition of discrimination
Article 5, the right to liberty and security
Article 8, the right to respect for private and family life
2.w: Article 9 protects freedom of thought, conscience and religion, including manifesting religion in worship and practice. Supporting Mr Rahman to pray is a direct application (HRA 1998 Sch 1).

n.1: Article 14 prohibits discrimination in the enjoyment of the other Convention rights; it does not itself create the right to practise religion.
n.2: Article 5 concerns liberty and detention, not religious observance.
n.3: Article 8 protects private and family life; religious practice is protected more directly by Article 9.

2.q: George, 86, has end-stage heart failure and lives in a nursing home. Over two days he has become harder to rouse, has stopped eating, and his knees look mottled. His breathing alternates between deep breaths and pauses. Which group of findings most suggests that George may be entering the last days of life?
o: Raised blood pressure, bounding pulse and increasing peripheral oedema
New fever, a productive cough and a respiratory rate of 26 per minute
Improved alertness, taking more fluids and fewer respiratory secretions
Mottled skin, Cheyne-Stokes breathing and a falling level of consciousness
2.w: NICE NG31 (2015) rec 1.1.2 lists signs that may suggest a person is entering the last days of life: agitation, Cheyne-Stokes breathing, deteriorating level of consciousness, mottled skin, noisy respiratory secretions and progressive weight loss, alongside increasing fatigue, loss of appetite and functional decline.

n.0: These suggest fluid overload or worsening heart failure, not the recognised signs that a person may be dying.
n.1: These findings point to a possible chest infection or sepsis that needs assessment and escalation; they are not the NG31 signs of dying.
n.2: NICE NG31 1.1.3 says improvement in signs, symptoms or function may mean the person is stabilising or recovering.

2.q: During an ABCDE assessment of Jordan, 30, who was admitted with a gastrointestinal bleed, you note a pulse of 124 beats per minute, BP 92/60 mmHg, cool peripheries and capillary refill of 4 seconds. Which assessment step are these findings part of?
o: Breathing
Circulation
Exposure
Disability
2.w: Pulse, blood pressure, peripheral temperature and capillary refill time are all assessed under C (circulation). These findings suggest hypovolaemia and need urgent escalation (NICE CG174 lists HR over 90, systolic under 100 and CRT over 2 seconds as indicators for urgent fluid resuscitation).

n.0: Breathing covers respiratory rate, effort, oxygen saturation and chest sounds, not perfusion.
n.2: Exposure covers full skin examination, temperature, wounds, drains and bleeding sites.
n.3: Disability covers level of consciousness, pupils and blood glucose.
